1:
Calvin opens on the largest scale, as the occasion that drew Jacob's whole house into Egypt, and asks by what hidden and unexpected methods God performs what he has decreed. Providence in itself, he says, is a labyrinth, yet when we connect the issue of things with their beginnings that admirable method shines clearly; what hinders us is our own indolence, since we either make fortune the mistress of events or else spread near and natural causes as veils before our eyes; he knows scarcely a more illustrious representation of providence than this history. Henry notes that all three patriarchs met famine in the land promised them, to try their faith and teach them to seek a better country, since we have need of something to wean us from this world. Clarke adds that famines were frequent before agriculture was well understood and Canaan peculiarly vexed, one in Abraham's time, another in Isaac's, a third in Jacob's.

That Jacob saw the corn is taken by nearly all of them as a figure. Clarke states the rule, that in Hebrew one sense is put for another, so seeing here means learning; Ellicott supplies the mechanism, a large caravan trade between Palestine and Egypt by which the report got abroad; Wesley says he saw the corn his neighbours had brought home; Gill allows either sight of men passing with it or common report. Gill also records from Jarchi the other opinion, that some Jewish writers would have him see it by revelation of the Holy Spirit.

The reproach to his sons is where they linger. Calvin explains the idiom: men are said to look one upon another when each waits for the other and, for want of counsel, none dares attempt anything, so Jacob censures an inactivity in which nobody provides for the present need. Ellicott sets it in the second rainless season, when flocks languish and household retainers grow enfeebled and begin to die of the low fever that follows famine, so the words mean simply, why are you irresolute? Henry expands the standing into five kinds — desponding as though there were no help, disputing which shall go first or come last, deliberating and doing nothing, slumbering as if there were nothing to do, delaying as if time were at command — and closes with a rule: never let it be said we left to tomorrow what we could as well have done today.

Their obedience draws observations. Henry notes that heads of families must not only pray for daily bread but lay themselves out with industry to provide it, and that these went down themselves rather than sending servants: none should think himself too great to take pains. Calvin makes the journey a proof of filial reverence, since envy of their brother did not keep them from leaving wives and children for a long road at their father's word; and their coming in a great crowd enhances Joseph's fame, since a man supplying all Egypt by measure could still relieve neighbouring nations. Ellicott turns the numbers over: either the households had been thinned by famine, or each brother took servants, if what they carried home was to be of real use; and since flocks and servants remained to them later, he concludes there was probably a little rain in Palestine, enough for milk and flesh but not for corn.

Two absences are noticed at the end. Gill explains that Benjamin is called Joseph's brother because he alone shared both parents with him, the one son of Rachel left and dearer since Joseph was lost, so the father kept him back. On the ten who went, Gill marks the title given them: not Jacob's sons, which they were, but Joseph's brethren, the men who had sold him into Egypt and were now going there to buy from him, and would bow before him without knowing it.
6:
Clarke traces the title given Joseph — shallit, an intendant or protector — to the root behind the Arabic sultan, the style later taken by the Mohammedan governors of Egypt. Calvin makes the same note but cares more for the office: holding supreme authority Joseph submitted to every laborious service like a hired servant, so that the higher a man rises the more fully he is bound to business, and those who combine leisure with dignity pervert the sacred order of God. Ellicott adds that Joseph sold by deputy, so only a party this large, each brother probably with attendants, would be reported to the governor in person. Then they bowed, and Clarke marks the irony: the precautions taken to void the dream of Genesis 37:7 fulfilled it, for there is neither might nor counsel against the Lord. Calvin presses harder: the conspiracy against the celestial decree was fruitless, the Lord restraining the obstinate as refractory horses are handled the more severely the more they kick.

The recognition runs one way. Gill assigns it to twenty-two years, a grown beard, princely dress, the Egyptian tongue, and the assumption that a brother sold for a slave was dead; Ellicott, noting the knowing is stated twice, adds that Joseph, seventeen when sold, had changed far more than they. Calvin adds that God's word may dwell in the heart yet be so smothered by affliction as to seem extinct, so Joseph's recalling the dreams here is itself notable.

The charge is read as plausible statecraft, not pretext. Clarke glosses the word as footmen or trampers, who buy corn while learning whether a land is defenceless enough to plunder, a frequent Arab custom still; Ellicott says the Semitic race was watched with distrust in Egypt, frontier fortresses having been built against such incursions, the nakedness of the land being its want of garrisons. Keil and Delitzsch quote Gerhard on the defence — spying being capital, it is unlikely a father would expose so many sons to death at once — which Gill, Clarke and Ellicott all make the force of one man's sons, Ellicott crediting Abravanel; and Clarke notes that Joseph took exactly the precautions of a stranger with every reason for suspicion.

Why he pressed so far is disputed. Henry insists it was no revenge but three ends — to enrich his dreams, to bring them to repentance, and to learn his family's state, which he could not ask as a friend without discovering himself, so asked as a judge; and reads the three days' ward as God's way with souls designed for honour, humbling them under a spirit of bondage before binding their wounds by the Spirit of adoption. Ellicott, answering the charge of harshness, says Joseph did nothing they did not deserve. Calvin allows two just causes, to regain Benjamin and to sift them lest a premature disclosure add a new crime, yet will not excuse the dissimulation, a fault human infirmity committed and divine mercy alone forgave, and warns that no private example licenses what God forbids in common. On the oath they separate. Clarke denies there is any oath here and faults the translators, since the brothers report it as a solemn protest; Ellicott says swearing by the king's life was ordinary in antiquity and only Gospel morality forbids it; Henry calls it the courtier's oath, more than yea and nay and therefore of evil, though it may have confirmed them in thinking him Egyptian; Calvin, distinguishing obtestation from oath, still finds in it the profane adulation of that court, the repetition showing how readily one who has sworn once swears again. Gill adds that the three days ended with no brother willing to carry such news home; Calvin, that the delay was not appeasement but meant to make them anxious for their brother's redemption, Joseph's fear of God being the fountain of every honest conscience.
18:
Gill reads the change of terms on the third day as the heart yearning under the assumed face: they could not agree who should go, so Joseph receded from his order. Ellicott sees the softening — nine imprisoned reduced to one — with care that they feel him in earnest, possession of Benjamin being the surest way of drawing his father down. On the ground Joseph gives, Clarke notes that the Hebrew runs literally I also fear the gods, the article marking the Supreme Being off from the gods of Egypt, and Ellicott adds that whatever Egyptian word Joseph used, he would take care Elohim was rendered to them, so they should know he worshipped their God.

The confession is where they concentrate. Henry treats conscience as a remembrancer: time wears out neither the guilt of sin nor its record, and men who made light of a crime and sat down to eat bread find it laid before them twenty years after, affliction being the means of that awakening; and of all their sins conscience selects the wrong done a brother. Clarke turns it on the reader — heard now, conscience may be the instrument of salvation; unheard, it becomes the never-dying worm. Ellicott adds a test: they were here suffering unjustly, and that the old sin should rise so readily is itself the mark of real repentance. Calvin goes furthest. Before affliction pressed them they were in torpor, speaking of Joseph's death without agitation; adversity is God searching men, dissipating illusions and extorting a confession they would gladly avoid, though it profits nothing unless he touches the heart. He notes too that they did not stop at the cause before their eyes but ascended to a remote one — looking only at the present injury they could have done nothing but complain, and despair would have followed. On the word he allows an ambiguity, the Hebrew covering both crime and expiation as piaculum does in Latin, and prefers punishment: they are deservedly refused because they refused their brother, a dictate of nature before Matthew 7:2 was spoken, and matched by Proverbs 21:13.

Reuben's interjection is read two ways. Henry lets him have his comfort as his brother's advocate, and draws the rule that a sin against admonition is the worse for it, and that when we share men's calamities it is a relief not to have shared their iniquities. Calvin hears a reproof, Reuben magnifying their fault by reminding them how late their repentance is. Ellicott clears them of one charge in passing: since they plainly believed Joseph dead, the accusation that they lied in saying one is not falls, Jacob using the same words later of Simeon. Clarke pauses on the interpreter, doubting whether the dialects had parted so far or whether Joseph affected ignorance to avoid suspicion. Then the weeping, which Gill ascribes to a tenderness that could no longer hold the stern countenance; Henry makes it the image of God's mercies toward repenting sinners, reason still requiring the stranger's part because they were not yet humbled enough; Ellicott says he melted at their first word of regret, mastering it only for fear of losing Benjamin. Why Simeon is chosen is only guessed: Henry and Wesley suggest the bitterest enemy, or the least humbled, bound before their eyes to work on them all, perhaps loosed once they had gone; Clarke reports the rabbinic tradition that Simeon bound Joseph and put him in the pit, making this retaliation; Ellicott takes him for the chief offender and supposes his confinement made easy afterwards. Calvin, who thinks him bold and fierce on the evidence of the Shechemites, defends the suspense in which the rest were sent away as fear for Benjamin and the house rather than malevolence — but will not let the severity become a precedent, since want of mildness may crush an offender with grief.
25:
The vessels get more attention than the corn. Clarke reads the word as their vessels, the large leather-lined baskets Sir John Chardin found still in use across Asia, covered against wet and sand, and distinguishes them from the smaller bag named later, which held the ass's provender; our word sack, he adds, comes straight from the Hebrew. Ellicott turns the distinction against the common notion that the brothers went down each with one ass and one sack, which must then explain why so insignificant a knot of men was brought before the governor. The word here covers anything corn can be put in; that at the verse's end is the travelling-bag each patriarch carried behind him on his riding ass, their men walking beside the laden beasts. He asks what nine sacks would do for households so numerous, and Clarke agrees, putting the asses at several scores if not hundreds.

Why the money went back is disputed. Ellicott rejects the brothers' construction, that it was a pretext for detaining them next time: Joseph cannot have wanted to frighten them, fear being the one thing likely to keep them from returning with Benjamin, so it was meant as encouragement and a sign of good will. Keil and Delitzsch find the motive simpler, that it was against Joseph's nature to trade with his father and brethren for bread, the road provisions given on the same principle, though he may have foreseen the alarm. Calvin supplies a third reason, that Joseph feared his father, already impoverished, would not be able to buy a second time. Henry alone reads it typologically: Christ, like Joseph, gives out supplies without money and without price, the poorest invited to buy — yet guilty consciences take good providences in a bad sense, putting wrong meanings on what makes for them.

On which brother opened his sack, Gill reports Jonathan and Jarchi for Levi, Aben Ezra for Reuben as firstborn. Clarke explains why only one found anything: the money lay at the mouth in his bag and near the bottom in the rest, who found theirs only on emptying them at home. Ellicott uses that to reconcile Genesis 43:21, where they tell the steward they all found their money at the lodging-place — not strictly accurate, but they needed only to show that all had found it and could not now return it. On the lodging-place Clarke warns that our word inn gives a false idea, there being no such houses in that desert then or now: travellers make for a well and keep watch by turns. Ellicott allows that a frequented route may have had protection built for beasts and attendants, but no more than walls and water.

Their fear is described physically. Clarke renders the Hebrew their heart went out, the spasm of a sudden fright, matching it with the English saying that the heart was ready to leap out at the mouth; Ellicott says the verse is far more poetical in Hebrew — their heart went forth, and they trembled each to his brother — and leaves them looking at one another in terror. Wesley supplies the reasoning: knowing the Egyptians abhorred a Hebrew, and charged already as spies, they expected no kindness and concluded a quarrel was being picked with them. Calvin asks why they did not suspect fraud and fresh snares from the man himself, and answers that one thought possessed them, that they were receiving what their sins deserved, so that God stood where Joseph might have; providence, he adds, being truly acknowledged only so, since unbelievers who call their misfortunes accidental merely exasperate their grief. He is harder on what they failed to do: the remedy was at hand had they returned to prove their innocence, but terror ended deliberation and each only increased the rest's trepidation, from which he concludes that numbers profit nothing unless the Lord preside.
29:
Ellicott reads their report as edited: they admit the lord spoke hard things, but pass over Simeon's bonds and the harsher usage, lest their father refuse to send Benjamin. Calvin defends the long repetition, since Moses means to show how anxiously they excused leaving Simeon in chains and how strenuously they pleaded for the youngest; hunger is a sharp dart, yet Jacob would sooner the household perished than let Benjamin go, which can only mean he suspected them. The story of the wild beast had colour enough, but he knew their fierce hatred of the boy, and for thirteen years had hidden the grief.

Calvin sees in the general discovery a measure of their fright, since not one had thought to look in his own sack after money was found in another's — men smitten with fear have no particle of wisdom until God quiets them. He is willing to fault Joseph: he did not consider sufficiently, and grieved the father whose poverty he meant to relieve, so that even the most prudent let something flow from their acts which they never wished.

Clarke gives the Hebrew as all these things are upon me, preferring the Vulgate's sense of evils falling back on him, loads that hasten his death; Ellicott agrees, burdens he must carry. Calvin hears anger under it: Jacob does not openly charge them with murdering Joseph, but speaks as though, two sons taken, they hurried to destroy the third, and says the evils fall on him alone, doubting they feel them with him. Henry turns the sentence over — it proved otherwise, and all these things were for him, working together for his good; through ignorance and weakness of faith we take for adversity what is really working for us the weight of glory. Clarke adds his doctrine of restitution: God pardons the penitent but exacts restitution through providence, and the brothers who sold a brother are captives now, the binder bound in his turn, conscience supplying prison, jailer and bonds.

Reuben's pledge divides them. Keil and Delitzsch take it at face value, the greatest and dearest offer a son could make a father. Clarke calls it a strange proposal but proof of an honest heart, and notes that scarcely a transaction involving Reuben fails to set his character in an amiable light. Henry is severe: he undertook without so much as if the Lord will, and foolishly bade his father slay two grandsons, as if their deaths could compensate a son's. Ellicott splits the difference: to read the offer literally is irrational, Reuben meaning only a strong assurance that Benjamin runs no risk, though it was feeble talk, of a piece with the man's general weakness. Calvin explains why so vehement a pledge was called for: they lay under suspicion over Joseph, and nothing less would allay their father's fear. Gill unfolds the refusal phrase by phrase: Benjamin as Jacob thought the only surviving child of Rachel, the Targums all reading the mischief as death, and the gray hairs meaning he would never lift his head again. Henry finds distrust in it, Jacob having never seen Joseph after leaving him with them: it is bad with a family when children behave so that parents cannot trust them. Clarke borrows Dodd's picture of the venerable father pleading, Benjamin at his side, impatient sorrow in every face but his, where there is only the bleeding anxiety of paternal love. Ellicott sees a man looking forward without hope to Sheol, clinging to Benjamin because Rachel had seemed to live on in Joseph, and notes that this grief has softened the brothers, who bear the favoured child no grudge. Calvin names the deepest burden: with no hope but the promised seed, and sons from whom no blessing could be looked for, Jacob had to keep believing he cherished a Church of which scarcely any appearance was left.
